text:
*Interview with Bastien Girard, établisseur, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Monsieur Girard. You were at the table this evening.

GIRARD: I was, Inspector, and I'd have done better somewhere else. Aurèle and I had words over the repeater before the soup had gone round. I wanted the rights to it. He wanted a price that would have ruined me, and he said so in front of his wife and his nephew, which I did not thank him for.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the rest of the evening, as you remember it.

GIRARD: After dinner I sat on alone in the dining room with the brandy. Nobody wanted my company, and I didn't want Dr Vauthier's, all cigars and Latin tags. When the temple struck ten, my watch showed four minutes to ten. I look at my watch the way a merchant looks at his till. It is the first thing I learned.

MATTHEY: And after that?

GIRARD: I wanted air and a smoke. I went out into the street to smoke at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, and I stayed under the front windows of the house. It was bitter. There is old snow in the gutter and the frost gets through your boots at this height. I walk in the cold when I want to think, and I was thinking about the price.

MATTHEY: You had a cigar with you.

GIRARD: A Brissago, the cheap sort. They draw like a chimney and taste like the stove. I'd barely got it going when the piano started up in the salon, just as I lit my cigar, at twenty-nine minutes past ten by my watch. I didn't know who was at it. I was in the street, Inspector. I know a sad tune when I hear one, though I'm no musician. It stopped at eighteen minutes to eleven by my watch.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything else from the house?

GIRARD: At twenty-six minutes to eleven by my watch I heard faint quick bells from the master's window up above, and the piano was playing all the while. I'd know a repeater's notes anywhere. Quick and light, like a fingernail run down a comb. I took it for his, because it was his. He spent four years on that movement and could never keep his mouth shut about it.

MATTHEY: Félix Monnier. Does he owe you money?

GIRARD: He does, and I'm not ashamed to say it. He would have had it put off, and I told him I'd not put it off past my own bills. He laughs when he's frightened, that boy, and he was laughing at dinner. I don't say that to hurt him.

MATTHEY: When did you come back into the house?

GIRARD: I came back in at fourteen minutes to eleven by my watch. The hall clock had just struck eleven and its face showed two minutes past eleven. I went up to Félix in the library.

MATTHEY: Did you speak with him there?

GIRARD: About the money, and about nothing. He had the brandy with him. I didn't stay long. I'd had enough of that house for one night.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Monsieur Girard. Please don't leave the town until I have spoken to you again.

GIRARD: I'm a man with a firm to run, Inspector. I'll be in Le Locle when you want me, and you'll find me there with my cigars.
